newsitem.title: OMAN: Oman sugar refinery plan expanded to 300-360,000 T.
newsitem.headline: Oman sugar refinery plan expanded to 300-360,000 T.

text.p: Plans to set up a sugar refinery at the heart of one of the world's biggest sugar-consuming regions have been expanded, with forecast annual capacity possibly doubled to 360,000 tonnes.
"We are now looking at 300,000-360,000 tonnes (a year)," sugar trader Ali Redha Darwish told Reuters on Wednesday.

He and seven other prominent Omani businessmen are planning to set up the $70 million National Sugar Refinery (NSR) at Muscat's Mina Qaboos harbour by October 1998 to cash in on the Gulf's huge appetite for sugar.
At about 30 kg per head, annual sugar consumption in the Arabian Peninsula is among the highest in the world.
Much of the sugar is imported from Europe. "The biggest losers (from the new refinery) will be Europe," Darwish said.

He and his partners will be competing in the region with the new Al Khaleej refinery in Dubai, which aims at 720,000 tonnes annual output, and a refinery in Jeddah, which plans to produce 500,000 tonnes a year from early 1997.
But Darwish thinks there is room for all of them.
"The Saudi refinery will cater to about 90 percent of the Saudi market. If they reach their target, the Dubai refinery will be covering about 50 percent of the Gulf without Saudi."
Demand for white sugar imports in the Gulf and Iran and Iraq, but excluding Saudi Arabia, is about 1.7 million tonnes.
"Even if the Dubai refinery comes to full production, there is plenty of room for both of us. We will have 1.1 million tonnes capacity between the two of us and demand of about 1.7 million tonnes."
Neighbour Yemen was "the ace up our sleeve", Darwish said.
The impoverished state imports about 600,000 tonnes a year mainly from South Africa, Thailand, Brazil and Europe, Darwish said, adding, "We have the advantage of proximity."

Besides the huge regional market for sugar, Darwish said recently high white sugar premiums, lower freight costs for raw, versus refined, imports and cheap energy costs in oil and gas rich Oman were important incentives.
But government approval to flatten a granite hill and build the plant within the port had not yet been secured and a final feasibility study was due soon.
Once it gets the go-ahead, the firm would float 40 percent of its shares and list on the Muscat stock exchange, he said.
